mcqs.question: Why does structured (JSON) logging scale better than free-text logging as log volume grows?
options: Structured logging removes the need for a buffer or queue stage
Structured logs are always smaller in bytes than free-text logs
Free-text logs cannot be stored in the same system as structured logs
Structured fields can be filtered and aggregated exactly, while free-text logs only support substring or regex search
mcqs.explanation: The scaling advantage is queryability: exact field filters and aggregations versus grep-style substring search. It isn't about file size, storage compatibility, or the pipeline's queueing stage, which are unrelated concerns.

mcqs.question: A service starts logging full request bodies 'for debugging' and a customer's card number ends up in the log store. What's the systemic fix?
options: Scrub or allowlist which fields get logged before they're written, rather than logging raw payloads by default, and review logging code for sensitive-field exposure
Increase log retention so the incident can be reviewed longer
Switch from structured to free-text logging to make the data harder to search
The fix is only to delete that one log line after the fact
mcqs.explanation: The systemic fix is preventing sensitive fields from being logged in the first place via scrubbing/allowlisting and code review -- not increasing retention (which makes exposure worse), changing log format (irrelevant to what's logged), or a one-time deletion that doesn't prevent recurrence.

mcqs.question: Why do many logging pipelines choose to drop log lines rather than block the application when the pipeline is overwhelmed?
options: Dropped lines are always recovered automatically later
Blocking would make the application itself slow down or stall waiting on the logging pipeline, which is worse than losing some log data
Logging agents are physically incapable of buffering to disk
Dropping log lines has no effect on incident investigation
mcqs.explanation: The core trade-off is protecting the application's own performance — a stalled app is worse than a gap in the logs. Dropped lines are gone, not recovered, agents can and do buffer to disk (that's the alternative being weighed), and losing lines absolutely can hurt incident investigation, which is exactly the cost of this choice.

mcqs.question: A compliance requirement says logs must be kept for 7 years for audit purposes but are almost never queried. Which storage tier fits, and why?
options: Hot tier, since compliance data must always be instantly searchable
Cold tier, since it's cheap to hold long-term and the audit use case doesn't need hot-tier query speed
No tiering is needed — all logs should use the same storage regardless of age
Warm tier, because compliance data is queried daily by regulators
mcqs.explanation: Cold tier trades query speed for low cost, which matches data that's rarely accessed but must be retained — exactly the audit use case. Hot tier's cost would be wasted on data nobody queries, uniform storage ignores real cost/usage differences, and audit data isn't typically queried daily.
